chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: lines that meet, lines that never meet, a line across two lines, drawing parallel lines, and the angle rules that follow. Every rule is reached by reasoning from one earlier fact, so an angle fact is never a thing to memorise.

points.title: Try first, name later
points.text: The hook video leaves two folded-paper lines open: do they meet if they are drawn longer? The words intersect, perpendicular and parallel arrive only after the student has looked at lines.

points.title: Reasoning and measuring are told apart
points.text: Every angle fact is first met by measuring, then justified from a straight angle being 180 degrees. A measured pair may be a degree or two off, and the plan says why.

points.title: One chain of reasons
points.text: Linear pairs prove vertically opposite angles; corresponding angles decide parallel lines; corresponding plus vertically opposite give alternate angles; corresponding plus a linear pair give interior angles on the same side.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic with one video per concept and a practice concept at the end; interactive tools appear only where handling the angles is the idea. The book's questions follow in their own topic, one question and one video per concept.

concepts.concept_name: Creases on a folded paper

content.text:
Across the Line
Use a piece of square paper and fold it in different ways. Now, on the creases formed by the folds, draw lines using a pencil and a scale.
You will notice different lines on the paper. Pick any pair of lines and observe their relationship with each other. Do they meet? If they do not meet within the paper, do you think they would meet if they were extended beyond the paper?

concepts.concept_name: Two lines that meet, and the four angles they make

content.text:
Let us observe a pair of lines that meet each other. You will notice that they meet at a point. When a pair of lines meet each other at a point on a plane surface, we say that the lines intersect each other.
Let us observe what happens when two lines intersect. How many angles do they form? Where line l intersects line m, we can see that four angles are formed: a, b, c and d.
Can two straight lines intersect at more than one point?
Activity 1: Draw two lines on a plain sheet of paper so that they intersect. Measure the four angles formed with a protractor. Draw four such pairs of intersecting lines and measure the angles formed at the points of intersection.
What patterns do you observe among these angles?

concepts.concept_name: Linear pairs and the straight angle

content.text:
If ∠a is 120°, can you figure out the measurements of ∠b, ∠c and ∠d, without drawing and measuring them?
We know that ∠a and ∠b together measure 180°, because when they are combined, they form a straight angle which measures 180°. So, if ∠a is 120°, then ∠b must be 60°.
Similarly, ∠b and ∠c together measure 180°. So, if ∠b is 60°, then ∠c must be 120°. And ∠c and ∠d together measure 180°. So, if ∠c is 120°, then ∠d must be 60°.
Therefore, ∠a and ∠c measure 120°, and ∠b and ∠d measure 60°.
Adjacent angles, like ∠a and ∠b, formed by two lines intersecting each other, are called linear pairs. Linear pairs always add up to 180°.

Worked example: Two lines cross. The angle a is 120°. Find b, c and d going round the point, without measuring.
1. a and b form a linear pair, so b = 180 − 120 = 60.
2. b and c form a linear pair, so c = 180 − 60 = 120.
3. c and d form a linear pair, so d = 180 − 120 = 60.
4. So a and c are 120°, and b and d are 60°.
Answer: b = 60°, c = 120°, d = 60°

concepts.concept_name: Vertically opposite angles, and a proof

content.text:
When two lines intersect each other and form four angles, labelled a, b, c and d, then ∠a and ∠c are equal, and ∠b and ∠d are equal! Is this always true for any pair of intersecting lines?
Check this for different measures of ∠a. Using these measurements, can you reason whether this property holds true for any measure of ∠a?
We can generalise our reasoning without assuming the values of ∠a. Since straight angles measure 180°, we must have ∠a + ∠b = ∠a + ∠d = 180°. Hence, ∠b and ∠d are always equal. Similarly, ∠b + ∠a = ∠b + ∠c = 180°, so ∠a and ∠c must be equal.
Opposite angles, like ∠b and ∠d, formed by two lines intersecting each other, are called vertically opposite angles. Vertically opposite angles are always equal to each other.
From the above reasoning, we conclude that whenever two lines intersect, vertically opposite angles are equal. Such a justification is called a proof in mathematics.

concepts.concept_name: Measuring and reasoning are not the same

content.text:
You might have noticed that when you measure linear pairs, sometimes they may not add up to 180°. Or, when you measure vertically opposite angles they may be unequal sometimes. What are the reasons for this?
There could be different reasons: measurement errors because of improper use of measuring instruments, in this case, a protractor; and variation in the thickness of the lines drawn. The “ideal” line in geometry does not have any thickness! But it is not possible for us to draw lines without any thickness.
In geometry, we create ideal versions of “lines” and other shapes we see around us, and analyse the relationships between them. For example, we know that the angle formed by a straight line is 180°. So, if another line divides this angle into two parts, both parts should add up to 180°. We arrive at this by reasoning and not by measurement. When we measure, it might not be exactly so, for the reasons mentioned above. Still the measurements come out very close to what we predict, because of which geometry finds widespread application in different disciplines such as physics, art, engineering and architecture.

Worked example: Imran measures a linear pair as 63° and 119°. Their sum is not 180°. Does that break the rule? What should the second angle be?
1. 63 + 119 = 182, which is 2° more than 180.
2. The rule of 180° comes from a straight line with no thickness; a drawn line is thick and the reading of a protractor can be off by a degree or two.
3. By reasoning, the second angle is 180 − 63 = 117.
4. So the measure 119° is 2° off, a measurement error, and the rule is not broken.
Answer: No; the second angle should be 117°, and the 2° is a measurement error

content.text:
Can you draw a pair of intersecting lines such that all four angles are equal? Can you figure out what will be the measure of each angle?
If two lines intersect and all four angles are equal, then each angle must be a right angle (90°).
Perpendicular lines are a pair of lines which intersect each other at right angles (90°). Lines l and m in the figure are perpendicular to each other.

Worked example: Two lines cross so that all four angles are equal. Find each angle, and say what the lines are called.
1. Two neighbouring angles are a linear pair, so together they are 180°.

3. All four angles are 90°, that is, right angles.
4. Lines that intersect at right angles are perpendicular, however the pair is tilted.
Answer: Each angle is 90°, and the lines are perpendicular

concepts.concept_name: Parallel lines, in pictures and around us

content.text:
Here are some examples of lines we notice around us. What is common to the lines in the pictures? They do not seem likely to intersect each other. Such lines are called parallel lines.
Parallel lines are a pair of lines that lie on the same plane, and do not meet however far we extend them at both ends.
Name some parallel lines you can spot in your classroom.
Parallel lines are often used in artwork and shading.
Which pairs of lines appear to be parallel in the figure of nine segments?
Note: It is important that the lines lie on the same plane. A line drawn on a table and a line drawn on the board may never meet but that does not make them parallel.

concepts.concept_name: Folding a sheet in half again and again

content.text:
Activity 2: Use a plain square sheet of paper (use a newspaper for this activity).
How would you describe the opposite edges of the sheet? They are parallel to each other.
How would you describe the adjacent edges of the sheet? The adjacent edges are perpendicular to each other. They meet at a point. They form right angles.
Fold the sheet horizontally in half. A new line is formed. How many parallel lines do you see now? How does the new line segment relate to the vertical sides?
Make one more horizontal fold in the folded sheet. How many parallel lines do you see now?
What will happen if you do it once more? How many parallel lines will you get? Is there a pattern? Check if the pattern extends further, if you make another horizontal fold.

content.text:
Worked example: A square sheet has two flat edges. Fold it horizontally in half again and again. Count the parallel lines, including the two edges, after one, two, three and four folds. What is the pattern?
1. Opposite edges are parallel, and adjacent edges are perpendicular.
2. After 1 fold there are 2 gaps, so 2 + 1 = 3 parallel lines.
3. After 2 folds there are 4 gaps, so 4 + 1 = 5 parallel lines.
4. After 3 folds there are 8 gaps, so 8 + 1 = 9 parallel lines.
5. After 4 folds there are 16 gaps, so 16 + 1 = 17 parallel lines.
6. Every fold doubles the gaps, so the number of lines is 1 more than the gaps, 3, 5, 9, 17, ...
Answer: 3, 5, 9 and 17 parallel lines; the gaps double and the lines are one more than the gaps

content.text:
Worked example: Fold a square sheet along one diagonal. Describe a fold that makes a line parallel to this diagonal and say why it is parallel.
1. Fold the corner that is not on the diagonal onto the centre of the sheet.
2. The crease is at right angles to the other diagonal, because the fold sends the corner straight along it to the centre.
3. The first diagonal is also at right angles to the other diagonal.
4. Two lines at right angles to the same line are parallel, so the crease is parallel to the diagonal.
Answer: Fold a corner onto the centre; the crease is parallel to the diagonal

concepts.concept_name: Perpendicular and parallel folds

content.text:
Worked example: A square sheet is folded in the middle both ways, the edges are folded to the centre line, and then two opposite corners are folded onto a centre crease to make triangles. Pairs of creases a and p, b and q, c and r are marked. Are they parallel?
1. a and p lie along folds that run the same way, so they lie on parallel lines.
2. b and q are both perpendicular to those lines, so b and q are parallel to each other.
3. c and r are the slanting edges of the two folded triangles. Both triangular folds are made against the same diagonal direction, so c and r are parallel.
4. So a is parallel to p, b to q, and c to r.
Answer: Yes: a is parallel to p, b to q and c to r

concepts.concept_name: Arrow marks and the square: notation

content.text:
Notations
In mathematics, we use an arrow mark (>) to show that a set of lines is parallel. If there is more than one set of parallel lines, the second set is shown with two arrow marks and so on. Perpendicular lines are marked with a square angle between them.

Worked example: A drawing has two flat parallel lines, two slanting parallel lines, and one upright line that crosses a flat line at 90°. How are these marked?

3. The upright line and the flat line are perpendicular: a small square in the corner between them.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q1: Draw some lines perpendicular to the lines given on the dot paper. There are two grids, each 3 dots across and 4 dots up. In the left grid, one segment is flat, 2 steps long, and another leans with 2 steps across and 2 steps up. In the right grid, one segment has 2 steps across and 3 steps down, and another is upright, 2 steps long.
1. Flat segment: an upright segment is perpendicular to it, so draw upright segments between dots (0 steps across, some steps up).
2. Leaning segment with 2 across and 2 up: swap the steps and change one sign, giving 2 across and 2 down. Draw leaning segments of 2 across and 2 down.
3. Upright segment: a flat segment is perpendicular to it, so draw flat segments between dots.
4. Segment with 2 across and 3 down: the perpendicular needs 3 across and 2 up, and the grid is only 3 dots, that is 2 steps, across. It cannot be drawn between dots on this grid, so it needs a wider grid or a set square.
5. Perpendicular lines need not be one flat and one upright: the leaning ones also meet at 90°.
Answer: Upright lines for the flat segment, flat lines for the upright one, lines of 2 across and 2 down for the leaning one; the 2-across-3-down segment needs a wider grid

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q2: Five shapes are drawn on a dot grid. Each corner is given as (across, down) from the top left. Shape 1: (0,0), (2,2), (2,4), (3,5), (0,5). Shape 2: (6,1), (10,1), (8,3), (4,3). Shape 3: (5,4), (7,6), (7,8), (5,8), (3,6), (5,6). Shape 4: (0,7), (3,7), (0,10). Shape 5: (5,9), (8,9), (11,7), (11,11), (5,11). Mark the parallel lines with arrow marks (a single arrow, double arrow and so on) and the angle between perpendicular lines with a square. (a) How did you spot the perpendicular lines? (b) How did you spot the parallel lines?
1. Shape 1: the side (0,0) to (2,2) and the side (2,4) to (3,5) both go 1 across and 1 down in each step, so they are parallel (single arrow). The upright sides (2,2) to (2,4) and (0,5) to (0,0) are parallel (double arrow). One right angle, at (0,5), between the upright side and the flat bottom.
2. Shape 2: (6,1) to (10,1) and (8,3) to (4,3) are both flat, so parallel (single arrow). (10,1) to (8,3) and (4,3) to (6,1) both go 2 across and 2 down, so parallel (double arrow). No right angle.
3. Shape 3: three pairs. (5,4) to (7,6) with (5,8) to (3,6) (single arrow). (7,6) to (7,8) with (5,6) to (5,4) (double arrow). (7,8) to (5,8) with (3,6) to (5,6) (triple arrow). Right angles at (7,8) and at (5,6).
4. Shape 4: only one right angle, at (0,7), between the flat side and the upright side. No pair of parallel sides.
5. Shape 5: (5,9) to (8,9) with (11,11) to (5,11) are flat, parallel (single arrow). (11,7) to (11,11) with (5,11) to (5,9) are upright, parallel (double arrow). Right angles at (5,9), (5,11) and (11,11).
6. (a) Perpendicular lines: a flat line and an upright line on the grid meet at a right angle.
7. (b) Parallel lines: segments that repeat the same steps across and down, so the gap between them stays the same.
Answer: Shape 1: two pairs parallel and one right angle; shape 2: two pairs; shape 3: three pairs and two right angles; shape 4: one right angle; shape 5: two pairs and three right angles. (a) Flat and upright lines meet at 90°. (b) Same steps, same gap

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q3

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q3: On dot paper, draw different sets of parallel lines. The line segments can be of different lengths but should have dots as endpoints.
1. Flat sets: draw two or three flat segments in different rows; they can have different lengths.
2. Upright sets: draw two or three upright segments in different columns.
3. Leaning sets: start at different dots and take the same steps, for example 1 across and 1 up, or 2 across and 1 up, each time.
4. Check each set: the steps are the same, so the lines keep the same gap and are parallel.
Answer: Sets of flat lines, upright lines and leaning lines that repeat the same steps, such as 1 across and 1 up, or 2 across and 1 up

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q4

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q4: Using your sense of how parallel lines look, draw lines parallel to the line segments a to h on dot paper (13 dots by 13 dots). Taking steps across to the right and then up or down: a is 1 across, 1 down; b is 2 across, 2 down; c is 3 across, 3 up; d is 4 across, 4 up; e is 1 across, 3 down; f is 1 across, 6 down; g is 5 across, 2 up; h is 10 across, 3 down. (a) Did you find it challenging to draw some of them? (b) Which ones? (c) How did you do it?
1. a, b, c and d lean at the diagonal of a square, so they are easy to copy by eye.
2. e, f, g and h have unusual steps, so they are harder to draw by eye.
3. Method: count the steps across and up of the given segment, start at a new dot, and take the same steps. For e: 1 across and 3 down; for f: 1 across and 6 down; for g: 5 across and 2 up; for h: 10 across and 3 down.
4. Because the steps are the same, the new segment keeps the same gap and is parallel.
Answer: (a) Yes. (b) The segments e, f, g and h. (c) Count the steps across and up and repeat them from another dot

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q5

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallel and perpendicular lines), Q5: Which line is parallel to line a, line b or line c? How do you decide this? Line a, line b and line c lean to the right. A steep line meets a at one end and b and c at its other end. The angles the steep line makes are about 30° with a, about 29° with c and about 33° with b.
1. Compare the angles the steep line makes: with a it is about 30°, with c about 29°, with b about 33°.
2. The angle with c is close to the angle with a; the angle with b is 3° more.
3. Equal corresponding angles mean parallel, so c is the line parallel to a.
4. Another way to see it: c stays the same gap from a, while b closes in.
Answer: Line c is parallel to line a, because the angles made with the steep line are about equal, 30° and 29°

concepts.concept_name: A transversal and its eight angles

content.text:
We saw what happens when two lines intersect in different ways. Let us explore what happens when one line intersects two different lines.
In the figure, line t intersects lines l and m. t is called a transversal. Notice that 8 angles are formed when a line crosses a pair of lines.
Is it possible for all the eight angles to have different measurements? Why, why not?
What about five different angles, 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2?
Since ∠1 and ∠3 are vertically opposite angles, they are equal. Are there other pairs of vertically opposite angles? We can see that there are a total of four pairs of vertically opposite angles and in each pair, the angles are equal to each other.
Thus, when a transversal intersects two lines, it forms eight angles with a maximum of four distinct angle measures.

content.text:
Worked example: A transversal t crosses lines l and m. The angles are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 going round the crossing with l, and 5, 6, 7, 8 going round the crossing with m in the same way, so that 1 and 3, 2 and 4, 5 and 7, 6 and 8 are vertically opposite. Can all eight angles have different measures? Can the five angles 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2 be all different?
1. Vertically opposite angles are equal: angle 1 equals angle 3, 2 equals 4, 5 equals 7 and 6 equals 8.
2. There are four pairs, so there are at most 4 different measures, and all eight cannot differ.
3. Among the five angles 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2, the angles 2 and 4 are a vertically opposite pair, so they are equal.
4. So these five angles cannot all be different.
Answer: No: at most four different measures; and 2 and 4 are equal, so the five cannot all be different

concepts.concept_name: Corresponding angles

content.text:
In the figure, we notice that the transversal t forms two sets of angles, one with line l and another with line m. There are angles in the first set that correspond to angles in the second set based on their position.
∠1 and ∠5 are called corresponding angles. Similarly, ∠2 and ∠6, ∠3 and ∠7, ∠4 and ∠8 are the corresponding angles formed when transversal t intersects lines l and m.
